title: A camel and a needle (Mark 10:23–31)
hook: with people it's impossible, but not with God

segments.voice: Yesterday, a good man ran to Jesus, and walked away sad. Your line was he loved him. Did you look at someone long enough to love them first? Day two hundred three. The end of the week.

The man with great possessions is still walking away down the road, and Jesus watches him go. Then he turns and looks around at his friends. In the King James Bible: "How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!" The disciples are stunned. In their world, wealth often looked like God's blessing. If the rich can't get in, who can? He says it again, more gently, calling them children. And then he reaches for the most ridiculous picture he can find. The biggest animal anyone in Galilee had ever seen. The smallest hole anyone had ever threaded. It's the kind of thing you'd say to make someone laugh out loud, and then go very quiet.
screen: `HE WATCHES THE MAN GO.` → `HOW HARDLY SHALL THEY.` → `THE BIGGEST AND THE SMALLEST.`

segments.voice: "It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God." People have tried hard to make this easier. You may have heard that there was a small gate in Jerusalem's wall called the Eye of the Needle, where a camel had to kneel and squeeze through. It's a lovely sermon illustration, but there's no evidence such a gate existed in Jesus's day; the story shows up many centuries later. Others noticed that the Greek for camel, kamēlos, is one letter from kamilos, a rope, and a few later copies say rope. But the oldest manuscripts say camel. He meant impossible. The disciples hear it that way too: then who can be saved? And Jesus looks at them and says: "With men it is impossible, but not with God: for with God all things are possible." The camel isn't squeezing through by trying harder. Something only God can do. Peter blurts out: we've left everything to follow you. And Jesus promises that nobody who has left home and family for his sake will miss out; they'll receive a hundred times over, homes and brothers and sisters and mothers, now. Only Mark adds two words: with persecutions. Then: many that are first shall be last, and the last first. Look back at the week. Who's the greatest? Not one of us. Salt. Marriage. Let the children come. A rich man who walked away. And a camel. Every day, the same upside-down shape: the last first, the child in the middle, the impossible possible.
screen: `NO NEEDLE GATE, NO ROPE.` · `THEN WHO CAN BE SAVED?` · `WITH GOD ALL THINGS ARE POSSIBLE.` · `A HUNDREDFOLD, WITH PERSECUTIONS.` · then, large: `WITH GOD ALL THINGS ARE POSSIBLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find something you'd miss, and give it away. Settle, and breathe. Look around in your mind at the things you own. Not the junk drawer. Something you'd actually miss. A good jacket. A book you love. Money you'd set aside for a treat. Pick one, and think of someone who'd be glad of it. Notice the part of you that tightens. That's the camel at the needle. If you pray, you can ask for help to open your hand. The bell holds the time.
A camel and a needle. The biggest animal, the smallest hole: impossible for people, but not for God.
screen: `A CAMEL AND A NEEDLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: all things are possible. Today, give the thing away, and let that be the small impossible you manage. Day two hundred three.

howItsDone: Christians often turn to this passage when talking about money and generosity; many give a regular share of their income to church and charity, and some traditions encourage giving away something valued, especially in Lent.

fork.setup: you're a disciple. you've just heard that a camel could pass through a needle's eye more easily than a rich man into the kingdom. you ask: then who can be saved? what does he say?
options: with God all things are possible.
fork.reveal: "With men it is impossible, but not with God: for with God all things are possible." not a smaller camel. a bigger God.

original.note: Greek: camel. a few later copies read kamilos, rope, but the oldest say camel.

trapdoor: what you thought: there was a narrow gate camels could squeeze through.
what it means: it's impossible for people, on purpose; only God makes it possible.
what a scholar hears: no ancient needle gate is attested, and the rope reading, kamilos, is a late variant.

sources.quoted: How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!

notes: Needle-gate story: commonly traced to medieval or later sources (sometimes to Theophylact, 11th century); script says 'many centuries later' and 'no evidence ... in Jesus's day'. Confirm.
kamēlos/kamilos variant: found in a few late manuscripts; confirm.
'In their world, wealth often looked like God's blessing' is a general claim; confirm phrasing.
'With persecutions' (10:30) is absent from Matthew and Luke's parallels. Confirm.
